# Skill Library

## Workflow

1. Query at the start of every task, and again whenever the work moves to a
   new language, framework, tool, file type or kind of work (tests, CI,
   release, docs, deploy). Do it even when the task looks well defined: you
   can't know which skills the library holds without querying. Summarize the
   task in 1–3 sentences (key technologies, file types, and the goal) and run:

   ```sh
   skill-library query -a <your-agent-id> "<task description>"
   ```

   Agent ids look like `claude-code`, `codex`, `opencode`, `cursor`,
   `gemini-cli`. An unknown id prints `Valid agents: …`; pick yours and run
   again. Query often: a query is cheap, a missed skill is not.

2. Read every `SKILL.md` listed (the `└ <path>` lines) **before** working on
   the task, and follow it. These paths are the only skills to use: don't look
   for skills anywhere else. `(always)` skills come back for every task; read
   them too. `No matching skills.` means continue on your own judgment.
3. If the output ends with `Your skills changed — tell the user:`, or the query
   succeeds but prints a note on stderr, pass it on to the user briefly.
4. A quick follow-up on the same task can reuse the skills already read; when in
   doubt, query again.

## When the query fails

If the query exits non-zero, tell the user the cause in a sentence and continue
the task without skills. Don't retry a query that keeps failing the same way.

- CLI missing (`command not found`): the user can set it up by following
  https://github.com/ianwijma/skill-library-skill#quick-start.
- Missing `SKILL_LIBRARY_TYPESAFE_API_KEY` or HTTP 401: the agent's environment
  needs a valid TypeSafe key (same setup link). Never print the key.
- Connection error or timeout: TypeSafe was unreachable (network, proxy or
  sandbox restrictions, not necessarily an outage). If your environment offers
  a way to request network access, use it, and respect a denial.
- Anything else: report the actual error message.

# Authored display-list lookup performance

The hosted exact-head jobs for PR161 (`43464683553/132020519726`) and PR163
(`43466555189/132027117925`) each failed only the unchanged mock playthrough
readiness deadline. They were advancing at frame64,000/level6/life971 and
frame62,000/level6/life868 respectively;150 other browser cases passed and4
were skipped in each. PR162's run was cancelled. These logs are preserved under
`test-results/artwork-stack-ci/`. No stopped progression or causal regression
is inferred merely from those timing failures.

## Baseline and one-variable candidate

A fresh current combined-source mock pilot at base `d7f27bf` passes locally with
all original inputs/assertions/deadlines intact. The passive10ms CPU sampler
locates a substantial share of self time in display-list lookup. Rendering only
occurs at milestones in this accelerated harness, so a per-frame mask-drawing
theory does not fit that caller. The local baseline does not reproduce the
hosted deadline failure; its timing is diagnostic evidence, not a hosted pass.

The sole candidate change replaces the authored `id:frame` string-map cache with
`DisplayListCache`: a WeakMap from actual SpriteInfo metadata objects to numeric
frame-indexed arrays. It stores only authored DisplayPlacement data, never live
clips, ages, parents, random streams or physical memberships. AssetPack, generic
effects and pickup numeric providers share the same helper. Existing frame
normalization and buildDisplayList remain; clear drops lookup rows only. No live
clock, object-retention, event-yield, input, entropy/provider, frame-cap, assertion
or timeout policy changes. There is no direct-WeakRef-loop or MessageChannel
experiment in the candidate.

An isolated actual-AssetPack comparison runs the exact old cache method against
the new method, with warmed queries and alternating order across five samples
each. Three million lookups per sample have identical placement checksums. Median
old/new times are237.04ms/75.01ms (ratio0.316). This microbenchmark alone does not
prove full-game timing. Its private code, raw rows and checksums remain under
`test-results/artwork-cache-performance/`.

The full mock pilot with the same passive profiler improves from147.25s to
110.37s (ratio0.7495), one fresh game per variant. **The entire serialized gameplay
proof is identical**, including all milestones/statistics, frame65,976, all six
upgrades, boss/badge/Continue and input digest3425647555. Both profiles, complete
reports and proof files are retained separately under
`test-results/artwork-pilot-profile/`; this finite sample does not establish
universal timing, original/Adobe, global-event/RNG or ordinary-input parity.

## Build/check attempts retained separately

The first private timing benchmark had an implicit-array type annotation error;
it is corrected without changing the workload. A concurrent Next build removed
generated .next/types during a rule-check attempt. Another Bun typecheck launcher
terminated with SIGSEGV before tests ran. Neither attempt is a passing rule gate.

The first unprofiled-pilot build reported an unhandled `ReferenceError: B is not
defined` before compilation completed and remained live. Its log, Next trace and
PID/start-time records were saved. Only that identified owned build tree was
terminated, and only this checkout's generated .next/cache was removed. A clean-
cache retry compiled successfully. No source/configuration, assertion, dependency
version or account setting was changed as a build workaround. Remaining checks
run sequentially after browser jobs to avoid generated-type races and timing
contention.

bun test-results/artwork-cache-performance/benchmark.ts

assertion, source frame loop, input sequence or deadline is altered. Browser
progression here is the existing accelerated adapter, not checkpoint6.2's
normal-time public-input acceptance. The supplied-art and sequential rule outcomes
will be recorded after their live handles finish; no pending result is green.

# Architecture

## Engine choice

[PixiJS](https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/components/application) supplies the WebGL renderer and scene graph. The game does not need a rigid-body physics engine, a tile map, or an entity framework: the recovered simulation uses authored tank parts, point-against-art collision, independent velocity axes, and frame timers. Keeping those rules in plain TypeScript avoids coupling them to a framework's physics or variable-time integration.

Next.js supplies the application shell, TypeScript build, and static delivery. Tailwind is installed through its PostCSS integration; stage-specific styling is kept in one stylesheet so original Flash coordinates can remain explicit. Pixi is imported on demand by rendered screens. No server-side game API or database is required.

## Ownership and flow

1. `AssetGate` accepts a local file or initializes procedural mock artwork.
2. `AssetPack` extracts images, sounds, vectors, font outlines, and sprite placements. It composes frozen previews and shared vector-leaf textures. It never executes ABC/ActionScript or calls retired endpoints.
3. `GameShell` owns the local profile, screen navigation, dialogs, and a `World` instance.
4. `GameViewport` owns input listeners, the Pixi renderer and cleanup. `MainStage` drives the shared `StageRuntime` fixed-step clock. Input is cleared on blur and gameplay pauses when hidden.
5. `World.step` advances one original game frame. `weapons.ts`, `projectiles.ts`, `actor-movement.ts`, `waves.ts`, and `tank.ts` implement separate systems. Beam contact, healer patient ownership, turret construction, and status callbacks/clocks are isolated in `beams.ts`, `healing.ts`, `turrets.ts`, and `status.ts`. Rendering and browser storage are absent from these rules.
6. `GameRenderer` positions the camera at the avatar, draws fields/entities/projectiles/pickups/effects, and updates `SwfSymbolView` display lists. `AssetPack` supplies matching animated alpha-mask hit tests.
7. React observes a revision counter, approximately ten updates per second at 50 FPS; it does not render every simulation frame.

`MainMenuMotion` belongs to each menu instance and advances on the shared `StageRuntime`. `MainMenuView` retains the supplied-SWF title and control clip trees through Settings/Credits visits; A stage-wide `MenuPointer` queries native retained geometry or procedural contours; DOM buttons retain keyboard access over the canvas. Per-frame rendering uses refs and stage subscriptions, while `GameShell` owns screen changes and the guarded overlay. A new menu instance resets its intro; closing a child pane preserves its title timeline.

The browser-owned `UpgradeMenu` service retains its pure motion model and captured
bitmap history across creator/viewer children. `World.onUpgradeMenuOpen` reports the
interface-phase opening without storing browser objects. Card selection calls
`placeUpgrade` synchronously, then presentation completion calls `finishUpgrade`;
direct creator returns use the progression-slot rule. Components observe the shared
service for paint and input state. [Frame ownership](upgrade-frame-reference.md)
documents fresh browser capture and the fixed cohort shared across Main, background
and child-menu phases. Main4 skips World.Run while attached artwork still advances;
explicit World events own background stop/resume independently of dialog mode.

`TankCreator.onLoad` passes its avatar/enemy mode and current limits to the local `TankViewer` screen. `GameShell` retains the editor return context and paused game viewport through that visit; the viewer's artwork and fades use the same stage clock. Selection constructs a fresh editor from the chosen design. Back reconstructs the current avatar or a new empty enemy, matching the recovered source routes. Viewer save/delete callbacks update the versioned local profile, and only completing the final guide page persists `tankViewerHelpSeen`. The viewer handles unavailable community search through the isolated service adapter.

The fixed stage wrappers clip overflow without becoming browser scroll containers, preserving the shared550×450 origin even when retained artwork extends beyond it. A primary creator workspace press closes Enemy Info while retaining its manual values. Dialog buttons remain text-only state layers: the native raster API has no static artwork to cache for their up/over/down records.

Creator input passes physical player coordinates through `core/display-transform.ts`: float32 matrices, signed twip translations, device-pixel mouse rounding, and the event-target/stage/reference Point conversions. The browser supplies the applied CSS transform and DPR; the numeric module has no DOM or saved-data access. `EditorDisplayState` separately owns transient clip x/y/rotation/scale. Drawing, hit tests, selection bounds and radial validation consume those getters, while tank codes and history retain raw saved fields. Drag membership/twin links update during movement and selected positions synchronize on release; each transform handle releases only its own field. Nudging advances both stores independently per frame; undo and rejected edits reconstruct clips from accepted metadata. Class measurement separately constructs its source snapshot from saved fields through display setters.

Marquee paint and its retained source flag have different lifetimes. The first release clears the rectangle; later editor mouse-ups still run `_‑bp` until a workspace click or `_‑JQ` rebind clears the flag. Selection samples combine clip positions with saved radius/scale, and the actual release point is independent of the last drawn rectangle. The earlier stage listener can clear selection before a slider's stage release copies its field. Delete instead acts at target mouse-up, while layering/centering and the extra nudge pixel act on the later click. Selection controls remain mounted while hidden, retaining that click and its accepted no-op history entry. Held nudge history is recorded before that click. Palette dragging and scrollbar dragging detach/rebind the workspace listener. Live selection refs preserve this ordering within a React event; the same native event is consumed once. Accessible range changes commit immediately and clear the retained marquee state. Workspace/transform cancellation restores the preceding gesture state and suppresses its trailing release.

Attached status marks are simulation state: their chosen part positions, rotations, variants, and replacement lifetime stay stable across frames and inactive fields. `SwfTankStatusView` consumes those choices without drawing random values or changing game rules. It holds variant frames while allowing nested clips to animate and applies the recovered infection color matrix to the complete tank view. Screen ink is an independently queued global effect; its lifetime and overlap do not belong to an avatar.

`assets/sound-window.ts` decodes native MP3 at its tag rate before AssetPack becomes ready, crops the positive source seek/sample-count window and prepares local16-bit PCM WAV blobs. Browser decoding stays outside simulation. `AudioManager` consumes events through its ten general sound slots and advances music from the shared stage before World steps, retaining source transition acceptance and muted-track memory. Fresh menu/game construction issues a distinct music request; profile settings only change enablement. Retained Settings, creator and nested viewer visits do not invent scene requests. Music completion restarts the same media carrier at full source volume without resetting the stage transition counter; replaced, muted and disposed voices cannot restart through stale callbacks. `simulation/collision-sound.ts` dispatches the recovered virtual hit-sound policy and callback enemy argument; World advances its shared hit cooldown at the successful Run tail, including pause. An interrupted listener skips that tail. The browser does not apply a second hit throttle.

`simulation/damage.ts` owns integer coercion, weaken, shield/forcefield absorption, recursive overflow, life changes, and the player hurt-channel latch. The latch advances with tank Run frames, independent of browser audio. `simulation/degradation.ts` owns the original incremental body-loss state (debt, total and cached minimum), keeping its selection order and healing behavior separate from rendering. Player bodies remain visible; surviving enemies/allies degrade, while enemy healing restores visibility before another degradation call. Both alpha collision and `TankView` consume the resulting hidden-part set.

The active frame checks progression in the interface phase, after existing-avatar controls/HUD and before field combat. Ordinary upgrades/downgrades therefore observe the previous field frame's final health. Level-zero damage starts its escape immediately. Primary input and passive weapons use separate category passes through `tickGuns`; passive shots are born after the field's bullet loop. Primary triggers run before field combat; primary cooldowns/aim and passive firing run in the later avatar phase. HUD readouts are captured in the interface phase, so later health/counter changes cannot leak into the same displayed frame. Shared secondary readiness retains its distinct zero reset frame and advances during transit. `WorldFlow` keeps raw execution state and its shared saved return state separate from attached dialogs. The selected Run branch finishes even when its interface opens a menu; crossing arrival can therefore restore state2 with a missing destination, while secondary-help Close writes ordinary state0 with its attachment still pending. The known source listener boundaries preserve those outcomes; browser mid-crossing pause is a separate existing adapter. Boundary detection precedes interface work; the initiating state0 frame still runs the avatar, while subsequent state2 frames run both fields without player status/passive updates. Arrival clears movement and the player shield, discards all registered effects/callbacks, and resets primary counters. The fidelity ledger identifies remaining source quirks, weapon callbacks and independent animation-clock work.

`simulation/actor-parents.ts` owns ordered physical actor children separately from enemy/ally Run arrays. Explicit attachment binds callback ownership; synchronization only updates ancestry/translations. Physical parentage does not select artwork lifetime. Raw host fixtures explicitly supply their omitted construction and attachment phases; production has no array-discovery fallback.

`simulation/field-runtime.ts` owns each live wrapper's shots, pickups, allies, removal queues and pending effects. `FieldCache` holds ordered actor references with frozen pose scalars, including raw queued deaths; attachment restores them into a fresh wrapper and replaces their parent/callback ownership. Logical map coordinates advance at attachment, separately from the current displayed field. The current and latest next wrapper receive combat Run; superseded next wrappers retain their last stage pose and independent artwork. `attachedFields()` exposes that display ownership separately from `activeFields()`. Completed outgoing wrappers clear shots/pickups before detachment; uncleared wrappers retain their detached collections. The destination keeps its already-running collections. Global effect clearing remains separate. A nested synchronous field context projects the same avatar and restores it with `try/finally`; world-level escape markers use current-wrapper coordinates even when next-field damage initiates the callback. Enemy and ally removal queues flush at the next field frame. Reparenting does not erase old array references or transfer an already queued callback. The live bullet loop still processes newly appended fragments in the same frame. See [crossing source contracts](crossing-source-reference.md).

`simulation/player-direction.ts` separates interface direction from acceleration and translation. It preserves the recovered heavy-tank turn helper, including exact-opposite ties, and updates aim/steering during transit without enabling movement.

`simulation/wall-timers.ts` models elapsed-millisecond Flash Timer callbacks separately from fixed-step part counters. The production viewport advances it from actual RAF elapsed time and passes zero elapsed milliseconds into each fixed stage step; deterministic callers can use `World.step(input, milliseconds)` (default20ms). The player launcher starts ten100ms callbacks; ordinary crossings and avatar replacement cancel them, while pause/jam/stun and death escape do not. Transit rejects insertion without replaying consumed callbacks. Managed Massive Cannon/shield timelines advance once per stage step even while paused, loop at their authored length, and are polled only by active world modes. Completion follows field bullets. This models source lifecycle; exact Flash Timer/event-loop delivery under stalls remains a runtime comparison boundary.

`simulation/pickups.ts` owns denomination selection, initial scatter, attraction and collection. Pickup state keeps scattering and the near-center collection latch separate from completion's forced attraction. The field performs alpha/latch collection before motion, preserves the original live-vector removal behavior, and advances its own collection sound counter after completion. Bounds deliberately consult the outgoing wrapper during transit, matching the source. `weapon-cycles.ts` stores the two special enemy firing cycles on each mounted gun, so jam/stun pauses their counters independently of visual age.

Non-player actors advance movement/sticky, jam, ordered parts, protection/effects, then ink/infection/weaken and boundary checks. NPC damage death and allied direct boundary exit share a deactivation phase in `World`: primary final callbacks run while data is live, before clearing data, setting the dead flag and recording the owning field callback. Damage supplies side-specific sounds/drops/infection before that phase; allied boundary exit supplies drops/pop and bypasses damage protection. Enemy callbacks queue next-frame removal; existing ally filtering retains its start/end timing. A stunned entry skips movement, parts and boundary for its complete reset frame while keeping protection/effects active. Enemy and ally arrays run independently without snapshots, allowing newly spawned enemies to run immediately. Player interface/passive ordering remains separate and its remaining source differences are tracked in the fidelity ledger.

`GameRenderer` keeps TankView instances keyed by actual Tank objects and reads each attached field's ordered `ActorParents.owned(field)` children. Per-field actor containers retain physical reparenting and child order, with the avatar as a separate sibling above them. Field, avatar, pickup and sibling projections now read retained instance matrices. World stays at (275,225); Main and user zoom remain separate ancestors. Effects read actual engine parents and retain views by Effect object identity. This remains a projected renderer, with complete field masks/order and exact live field queries still unfinished; see [the retained renderer boundary](retained-renderer-reference.md). `TankView` mounts only actual `displayChildren`, keeping an empty deactivated outer container until explicit actor detach; native status/protection and detached part roots retain their supported identities.

`render/tank-view.ts` paints a runtime tank independently of camera and simulation clocks. The game renderer and `TankPortrait` use it for the same current mounted-part rotations, visibility, animation pose, status and protection. The portrait owns a temporary transparent Pixi canvas above the paused field, at the original tank scale. Leaving the screen destroys that canvas and its texture store. `core/tank-info.ts` supplies source class/weapon formatting and frame-based entrance/retraction; its placements, TextField metrics and font ascent come from the HUD importer. Info does not export a reconstructed static design in place of the current pose.

`core/win-screen.ts` supplies the source preparation/fade clock independently of gameplay. `WinPanel` consumes static text/art and button frames loaded into `AssetPack.uiFrames`; it has no invented statistics. `tools/import-win-geometry.ts` preserves authored positions and alpha values while filtering the retired pack-manager promotion. The separate visual-fixture viewer mounts the production panel for browser checks. The clock records original blur-pass timing, but shared CSS blur still approximates the original repeated BitmapData filtering.

## Invariants

- Simulation units are pixels/frame, degrees, and frame counters. Do not multiply recovered constants by wall-clock delta.
- The stage is 550 × 450; rendering scales to fit without changing world dimensions.
- Health and progression are the same resource. Kills alone do not grant XP.
- The level life curve is `[50, 100, 170, 250, 400, 800, 2000]`.
- Mounted primary cooldowns are independent; secondaries share their maximum mounted rate.
- Field persistence owns living enemies and their exact runtime state. Inactive fields do not keep simulating.
- Recovered catalog designs are immutable templates. Runtime health, timers, removed carrier parts, and hidden bubbles live on `Tank` instances.
- Flash artwork is optional input. Mock mode must remain playable without a file.
- Map connections are completed traversal history, independent of grid adjacency and field generation. Each unordered pair is stored once. Cleared fields remain valid destinations.
- Camera zoom changes renderer scale and inverse pointer mapping together; simulation coordinates and the fixed HUD keep their original dimensions.

## Extending the game

- Add a part definition in the catalog, an implementation in the relevant combat/AI system, and a recovered symbol or mock view. Keep part IDs stable for code compatibility.
- Keep data importers reproducible. Derived JSON is checked in so the research repository is not a production dependency.
- `services/extensions.ts` contains typed interfaces for community tanks, accounts, parts packs, medals, platform stats, and ads. Replace the offline adapters to restore those systems without adding endpoint logic to gameplay.
- `services/profile.ts` validates versioned local JSON. The persistence boundary is replaceable; no component needs to know Flash SharedObject internals.
- `services/tank-code.ts` implements the original AES-128-ECB/PKCS7 tank format using Web Crypto's CBC primitive blockwise. It is a compatibility codec, not an account/security mechanism.
- A future renderer can consume the same `World`; a replay/test harness can call `World.step` with seeded input without a DOM.

## Asset lifetime

`Tank.age` follows active actor Run. `Tank.artAge` follows the separate World-owned artwork lifetime, including pause, control suspension, cached actors, directly removed retained actors and replaced avatars. `simulation/actor-artwork.ts` explicitly registers constructions and keeps weak object references, taking the ENTER cohort before Main work so inside-ENTER births hold their initial pose. Attachment/Run-array edits cannot construct, reset or rediscover clocks. Already materialized mounted trees subscribe through the numeric weak bridge in `core/actor-artwork.ts`, so removed roots and independent descendants advance without paint/contact reads. AssetPack still lazily constructs mounts with host entropy; this bounded correction does not complete constructor/pose/provider parity. See [the implementation boundary](actor-artwork-lifetime-reference.md). Native painting, part alpha tests, status/infection visual origins and forcefield mask clips use that stage age. Status durations, infection damage, weapon counters and forcefield recharge retain their active clocks. Shield film has26 frames independently of its25-frame cleanup callback; shield hits stop at16 and can finish after immunity ends. Forcefield frame jumps follow the authored1/25/35 scripts on the stage clock.

`core/protection-size.ts` preserves TankData's ordered axis-record algorithm, including ties and all-centered NaN. The browser binds `World.protectionRadius` to `AssetPack`'s transformed live Script bounds; headless callers can inject geometry, with stored-radius estimates as the default. A shield mount caches its first measured diameter, while the current hit clip retains the last mount-created diameter. `AssetPack` separately creates a fresh full-design forcefield mask pose tree and caches its initial sizing before stage advancement. Native width/height NaN assignments retain authored scale; forcefield sizing uses uniform width scale. Turret shields keep the separate gameplay-radius rule. Mock parts supply procedural raster dimensions to the same ordering rule.

The supplied SWF is held only for extraction. Projectile and pickup display lists share the same vector textures as tank views. Music fades advance on the shared stage clock, including in menus and while gameplay is paused. Audio Blob URLs are owned and revoked by `AudioManager`. Pixi textures and display trees are owned by `GameRenderer`; changing files, leaving a run, and unmounting remove listeners and release rendering resources. The asset pack keeps shared raster/font/timeline caches for the current selected file and clears them when replaced.

The shell owns a reactive audio-manager instance so the viewport receives the loaded pack's audio service. Pointer/key gestures retry suspended music on the current element. Mock audio is generated locally as short PCM WAVs, including a quiet music loop, and uses the same channel limits, mute controls, and cleanup as supplied SWF audio. Protection views use shared vector leaves and a cloned design mask; changing a design rebuilds its cached tank view.

The parser was adapted from `research/swf-browser-extraction/`. Corrections made here cover matrix byte alignment and shear order, `PlaceObject3` flags, retained color transforms and removal events, shape pen origins, appended style tables and paint layers, joined fill boundaries, normalized SVG view boxes, font outlines/advances, and masked sprite composition. Matrix semantics were cross-checked against [FFDec's input reader](https://github.com/jindrapetrik/jpexs-decompiler/blob/master/libsrc/ffdec_lib/src/com/jpexs/decompiler/flash/SWFInputStream.java) and [affine transform implementation](https://github.com/jindrapetrik/jpexs-decompiler/blob/master/libsrc/ffdec_lib/src/com/jpexs/decompiler/flash/exporters/commonshape/Matrix.java).

Morph placements retain their unsigned 16-bit ratio. `morphShapeAtRatio` resolves geometry, bounds, colors, gradient matrices/stops/focal values, and line widths; previews and collision use the same resolved geometry as live views. `morph-raster.ts` rasterizes generated leaf paths synchronously with Canvas2D so frame changes do not wait for image decoding. Its recent-raster cache is limited to eight million pixels. Live morph textures are reference counted by `GameRenderer` and released when their last view changes ratio or is destroyed; static vector leaves remain shared for the run. Morph structure and edge pairing were cross-checked against [FFDec's morph implementation](https://github.com/jindrapetrik/jpexs-decompiler/blob/master/libsrc/ffdec_lib/src/com/jpexs/decompiler/flash/tags/base/MorphShapeTag.java).

`tools/visual-fixtures.ts` builds a separate development viewer with deterministic world snapshots. It uses the production asset pack, simulation, and renderer; native SWF loading remains local. Browser tests compare contact masks and construction states there without adding debug routes or globals to the shipped application.

`simulation/editor-selection.ts` contains pure creator operations: ordered additive selections, faded twin membership, marquee sampling, transforms, ordering, and unlink/delete behavior. `simulation/editor-validation.ts` owns source-ordered aggregate checks against explicit class/budget values. `simulation/editor-history.ts` retains independent accepted part snapshots, including setup/import and accepted no-op operations; enemy statistics remain outside undo. `TankCreator` owns pointer capture, transient drag state, class-update timing and drawing. Selection and faded state are never exported as tank data. Browser coverage reads nonvisual design metadata after actual pointer interactions in both asset modes.

Prepared native creator819 background frames apply a scoped minimum-stroke width through the verified positive uniform placement tree. They paint in a registered decorative image behind the input/part canvas so the two-pixel raster padding preserves the complete border. This adapter leaves authored geometry, ordinary SVG/raster calls and Script/contact bounds unchanged; it does not model Ruffle tessellation-cache history.

`simulation/editor-drag.ts` advances a creator drag one pointer event at a time. It owns per-part pointer sides, the first-move reference offset, the axis lock, merge/delete decisions, and new mirrored twin insertion. Each advance returns new parts and selection state without mutating its input. The component starts on the first delivered move event without a displacement threshold, including zero delta; only a press with no move event retains ordinary click selection toggling. It retains the source's axis-lock flag across gestures, records accepted drag releases including no-op snapshots, and restores the starting design/selection on pointer cancellation. Browser coordinate arithmetic does not yet reproduce every original Point/display-setter precision boundary.

`simulation/editor-placement.ts` creates transient preview geometry, applies the three-pixel axis snap, and filters each dropped member against the design bounds. Palette choice, the in-progress preview gesture, and selection of placed parts are separate editor states. The browser component owns pointer capture and the keyboard alternative; dropping an object commits one design change without selecting it. Part radii come from authored symbol bounds, excluding the raster padding used for antialiasing.

`tools/reference-player.ts` serves a separate loopback-only original SWF viewer with development dependency Ruffle 0.7.1. It shares the SWF decompressor, serves WASM with the correct MIME type, and accepts a browser-local file or explicit `BT3_SWF_FILE`. `reference-browser.ts` owns a headless Chrome/CDP instance with the stack size this movie needs; `reference-input.ts` uses Node Playwright for native coordinate input and stage captures. Ruffle is never imported by `src` or included in the Next.js output. The optional original-runtime smoke test is enabled with `BT3_REFERENCE=1`; it complements simulation tests rather than establishing whole-game parity.

`simulation/editor-palette.ts` owns affordability, unlock state, source row ordering, and default selection independently of placement. Affordability checks one object; symmetry and final design validity are handled by placement and save validation. An unaffordable unlocked row is dimmed but remains selectable.

`render/creator-artwork.ts` reuses `SwfSymbolView` in one offscreen Pixi renderer, copying its transparent frame into the creator's design and preview canvases. Each placed part owns its own timeline birth frame; moving/scaling/selecting it does not recreate the clip. Dropping transfers draft views into the design so their animation continues. The frame clock follows the selected FPS, stops advancing while hidden, and stays outside React state. Pointer alpha tests consume each part's retained visible pose. Class measurement and saved designs continue to use their separate static snapshot and numerical geometry.

`CreatorArtwork` also owns an independent details layer. It measures a fresh clip before animation, caps its dominant dimension at48px once, and retains that scale through subsequent frames. Clearing the layer destroys its clips so a new detail focus restarts construction. Full-size palette previews retain their own instances and scale. Supplied-SWF loading caches the details static panel, both arrow poses, selection icon and popup; named fields and dynamic children remain outside these static rasters. The live part-details component uses these caches; selection-info UI uses the same retained cache.

`render/swf-textures.ts` owns leaf textures and reference-counted morph textures for both the game and creator renderers. Each renderer has its own store and releases it with its display trees. No animation frame atlas is generated, and closing the creator cancels its frame callback and destroys its offscreen WebGL resources.

`assets/clip-timeline.ts` runs the recovered stop, jump, rounded-random, and Y-branch actions. `assets/swf-clip.ts` owns the retained child tree and advances every elapsed stage frame, including child construction/removal while a parent is stopped. It has no DOM or Pixi dependency. `SwfSymbolView.updatePose` paints that tree; collision reads the same placements, masks, and morph ratios through `AssetPack.hitClip`.

`assets/glow-kernel.ts` and `assets/swf-color-transform.ts` hold numeric filter rules independently of Pixi. `SwfSymbolView` retains each placement's ordered glow filters, isolates authored bitmap-cache boundaries, and applies accumulated color after a filtered capture. Unfiltered branches pass color to their leaves. Embedding views supply runtime/parent alpha explicitly so Pixi ancestors do not attenuate the capture. `SwfGlowFilter` owns the repeated horizontal/vertical GPU passes and pooled scratch textures; `SwfColorFilter` applies the final bitmap transform. Contact and Script bounds retain their separate geometry. The development-only byte-image oracle and gallery test the rendering without entering the shipped game bundle.

`AssetPack.partClip` caches poses in a weak map keyed by runtime tank and resets them when its design changes. Each part has a stable private random stream derived from the tank/instance key, so repeated rendering or collision queries do not reroll animation or consume gameplay randomness. Creator clips use their own retained instances and normal random draws; the forcefield's cloned silhouette also owns independent instances. Numeric frame actions are generated from complete recognized source methods. Unsupported classes are reported, and importing fails if an unsupported frame method becomes reachable from a catalog part.

`core/minimap.ts` holds the imported layout and the compact/large/hidden state helpers. `render/minimap-view.ts` owns the native map shell, retained dot clips, traversal graphics, and clipping; it sits outside the world camera transform. Entries detach before an authored frame swap so replacing `map_mc` cannot destroy retained traversal artwork. The mock renderer follows the same control cycle and spacing. `WorldMap` supplies only the accessible cycle button and a screen-reader description; opening the map does not create a dialog or pause the simulation.

`core/hud.ts` owns health/fire idle clocks and easing in original simulation frames, ordered primary grouping, and fill calculations. `render/hud-view.ts` owns the native life/fire clip trees and their dynamic device-text children; mock mode draws the corresponding simple geometry. Both stay outside the camera transform. `GameHud` retains accessible health text and interactive controls, without React updates or CSS transitions driving the bar animation. `tools/import-hud-geometry.ts` imports only numerical origins, layout heights, and TextField metrics from the source SWF; artwork remains browser-local.

`core/edit-slider.ts` advances the source's distance-scaled entrance/retraction in simulation frames. Completion and field attachment trigger it; a settled tab reflows when the map changes size. `render/edit-slider-view.ts` paints the three native variants, including static text leaves. `EditTankControl` reads the model to move its transparent native-button bounds without React frame updates. Its DOM disabled state follows the model; React does not hold a conflicting fixed disabled prop. Clicking opens the original confirmation, then same-level replacement choices. Editing or selecting a replacement rebuilds the current progression slot at its initial health; canceling the creator resumes the run.

`core/tutorial.ts` selects a stopped caption frame using the unique-field count before attachment increments it. Every attachment, including a revisit, replaces the destination's guide. `render/field-captions.ts` retains the original static text/logo clip for each active field, below tanks, with no field-radius scaling. The field camera moves it through crossings; pausing does not remove the artwork. `tools/import-tutorial-art.ts` imports frame IDs, numerical positions and decoded fallback text. The original glyphs, colors and font outlines come from the supplied SWF. Mock mode spells out the separate W and mouse glyphs in readable fallback text.

`core/field-visit.ts` models the per-attachment completion latch independently of cached `Field.cleared`. `World` owns one current visit and a fresh destination visit during transit, checking both in source order and transferring the latch on arrival. Empty revisits increment completion statistics once per attachment without adding duplicate map paths. The initial wrapper is special; attaching home again is an ordinary visit.

`World.rebuildPlayer` owns the replacement-only secondary-help trigger and early seen latch. `GameShell` persists that event in the validated local profile; initial saved-avatar construction does not trigger it. A dedicated world mode freezes simulation while `SecondaryHelpPanel` displays the original static artwork and button frames loaded by `AssetPack.uiFrames`. Its generated placement data shares the HUD importer; the regular modal scrim is disabled so the authored white veil remains intact.

`core/tactical-hud.ts` holds fixed-stage snapshots for Radar, Health Readout and allied health. Their clocks differ: the interface updates ally rings through travel, while avatar passive parts retain their last snapshot until active again. Jam clears passive output and stun retains it. `render/tactical-hud-view.ts` paints native116/1999/2194 clips outside the camera, overwriting enemy fill scale and preserving source widths/heights. Reused clip trees keep stable textures; obsolete indicators are destroyed. `GameHud` exposes readout counts to assistive technology. Browser settings feed the simulation's numerical view zoom without DOM dependencies.

`core/target-lock.ts` defines the disabled parts-pack targeting boundary. No shipped part registers locks, and base Q input does not alter homing or auto-cannon targeting. A future pack can supply its own controller; World invokes cycle, preserved-capacity field reset, and zero-capacity avatar-replacement reset hooks. Lock-on projectile artwork alone does not establish an available weapon or its part ID.

Apocalypse calls the source's control-suspension state, separate from a normal pause or field crossing. `World` continues collapse/effect clocks while leaving the HUD snapshots and idle/edit motion frozen. Enemy Health Readout removes bars on entry; radar may persist. Editing is unavailable during collapse. The deterministic native fixture compares complete HUD pixels across20 effect frames so a renderer or clock regression cannot silently reintroduce motion.

`simulation/effects.ts` maps projectile callbacks to source effect identities independently of damage. `tools/import-effect-art.ts` regenerates their symbol IDs and frame counts without exporting artwork. Each field owns an effect request queue, flushed after its combat, pickups and completion checks. Registered effects belong to the outgoing engine layer until field promotion; destination requests retain their supplied local coordinates, matching the shared source engine. Arrival clears registered clips and callbacks. Effect ages advance on the stage clock even while gameplay is paused, while engine polling removes clips only on active gameplay/collapse frames. Massive Cannon/shield completion callbacks retain their separate managed timelines.

`render/combat-effects-view.ts` owns lower, upper and screen native effect containers and shared-texture MovieClip trees. The empty rocket-trail `line_mc` receives its dynamic two-pixel segment; the surrounding authored timeline supplies its 25-frame fade. Mock mode draws the same segment with a procedural fade and uses simple rings for the other source-defined effects. Ordinary damage/death and area damage do not independently create visual effects. Native artwork remains runtime SWF input, including all 12 newly reachable effect roots.

`simulation/projectile-contact.ts` handles the base current/backward-half-step mask tests and Massive Cannon's cardinal width samples before movement. It retains the friendly enemy-layer gate and source hit-memory behavior. Collision callbacks run before direct damage and can create effects, pickups or area damage independently. `tools/import-projectile-flags.ts` recovers constructor flags through source inheritance into `data/projectile-flags.json`; acquisition and area cleanup use those flags instead of inferring behavior from projectile kind. Dynamic mine arming overrides its Seeker flag.

`simulation/bubble-buster.ts` stores only the copied movement vector in `Projectile.deflected`, modeling base Run state2. It selects the first enemy clip in live array order using strict distance and Script width; later Busters may overwrite the same vector. Subtype aiming/contact/fuse polls stop, while retained stage artwork continues. Movement precedes the virtual wall check, which is skipped for stopped turrets (the shipped live `_‑PJ=false` case). Beams never expire at this boundary, ricochets expire without bouncing or reporting a miss, and Apocalypse uses the stroke-inclusive background radius425.25 rather than its fill radius423.75. Turret Setup initializes its movement before its first interception; interception uses copied vectors for deflected incoming shots, and owner validity follows field attachment rather than the death flag. Infection's shipped NaN acquisition failure is explicit in `infection-projectile.ts`; setup and first-Run effects/removal use the regular field queue. Leech creates a forced value1 pickup, leaving movement, collection accounting and healing to the pickup system.

`assets/projectile-bounds.ts` composes native leaf transforms into field-coordinate Script AABBs independently of raster painting. It retains mask/transparent children, declared morph start bounds, dynamic beam lengths and turret orientation. `GameViewport` binds `World.projectileBounds` to the supplied asset pack; width-based Massive Cannon/Buster checks derive from that same bound. Known empty authored frames carry an explicit empty flag and zero width; mock mode and absent native symbols use imported authored projectile bounds when known, with procedural bounds only for unknown symbols. Simulation-only callers can supply their own geometry without loading Pixi or a DOM.

`simulation/projectile-boundary.ts` centralizes the source virtual `IsOutsideOfBubble` dispatch and session-local friendly/enemy missed-shot counters. Ordinary strict radius415×scale checks report on each invocation; normal ricochet reports separately at its seventh outside event. `Projectile.missExempt` is the independent `_‑MB` flag, not inferred from the hit-ID set. Friendly base, piercing, Whip, Repulsor and Spinner set it at their recovered contact phases, including after explicit removal cleanup where required. Apocalypse starts exempt. Non-wall expiry, wipes and cleanup do not invent misses. No original UI/save consumer was found, so counters remain internal.

`simulation/mines.ts` separates stationary mines and seeker-mine contact/scatter/arming/homing from ordinary projectile motion. A mine stores its last movement vector for source half-step contact. `projectile-timelines.ts` owns weakly keyed retained `SwfClip` trees and advances roots and children on the independent stage clock, including pause and deflection. `mine-timelines.ts` retains a compatibility export. `Projectile.artPose` supplies the same placements to drawing, pixel contact and Script bounds; `artFrame` exposes the root frame for source polling. `tools/import-projectile-clips.ts` imports only numerical display-list metadata for seven projectile roots and their reachable clips. Effective frame-script bindings replay constructor registration around super, preserving the Whip base overwrite. Source numeric mine IDs/counts/labels and inherited frame actions are imported reproducibly; the ally mine's empty blinking frames are preserved.

`simulation/mine-layers.ts` stores each mounted gun's raw seeker references or ordinary `{mc,x,y}` wrappers. It preserves stale raw references, birth/current-coordinate cap distinctions and the source's caught owner-level cleanup failure. `World.removeBullet` centralizes removal plus this reference bookkeeping. Ready-for-delete projectiles skip Run and are removed after the live bullet loop; completion schedules a following-Run wipe. Death-spawned mines bypass cap bookkeeping. No renderer or browser service manages mine lifetime.

`starburst.ts`, `spinner.ts`, `repulsor.ts`, `sapper.ts` and `avatar-seeker.ts` isolate the subclasses whose phases differ from base movement/contact. Weakly keyed counters retain Starburst fuse, Spinner firing and Sapper master/health state independently of visual age. Base deflection bypasses these counters. Repulsor stores its active-update alpha in `Projectile.artAlpha`, so pause/deflection do not accidentally fade it through elapsed visual age; native and mock rendering consume the same value. Sapper initialization immediately steers and holds its outbound root frame, while per-mounted-gun references prevent one gun from suppressing another.

`create-projectile.ts` supplies fresh base state for helper shots. Starburst fragments, Spinner helpers and Converter replacements receive no copied hit memory, status, scale, anchor or subtype callbacks. Their source has no age fuse. Orbital/turret helper construction also no longer imposes an invented long timeout. `hit-location.ts` caches the source's nearest authored detail (including non-body parts and first ties) per immutable design, then projects it using the current hull pose. Camera zoom does not change these simulation distances.

`converter.ts` uses the separately imported RotateTowardTarget flag, not the Seeker flag. It scans the live array, appends fresh avatar seekers and flushes removal without original-shot impact callbacks. `avatar-seeker.ts` preserves the shipped first-entry retargeting bug and Setup-time homing/removal. Converter target selection retains its separate biased random index. These paths have no renderer dependency; their native/mock gallery extracts the actual production projectile layer into a six-panel development-only image.

`simulation/whip.ts`, `grow.ts` and `flak.ts` separate active Run state from retained stage playback. Whip samples the named primary child's registration points at its previous location before following the emitter, retaining launch rotation. Grow changes explicit scale/alpha only during active movement and removes itself immediately on the next Run after becoming transparent. Flak polls its current root frame for its blast/removal, so paused playback can skip the blast entirely. Sapper holds root frames while child clips continue. The shared display-list builder has no browser dependency; generated metadata contains no raster, vector paths, fonts or audio. Exact original event-loop/constructor interleaving remains a runtime comparison boundary.

`core/tank-identity.ts` retains exact supplied/imported encrypted tank-code identity for source roster lookup. Builtin codes are regenerated with the numerical designs by `tools/import-reference-data.py`; JSON/mock designs use a canonical full design/part serialization. `createTank` caches that identity at birth, just as `strTankCode` remains independent of mutable runtime data. `UnitRoster.lookupKey` scans keys in source sort order and returns the first exact identity match; classification does not infer archetypes from weapon costs, display names or IDs.

`FieldRuntime.enemyRemovals` separates the immediate death callback/total-kill count from removal-time archetype counters and medal checks. Ordinary field updates drain the previous queue before actors; source area/piercing/Repulsor cleanup drains it immediately. Apocalypse damages through protection and discards the wrapper without draining category medals. Medal thresholds retain source equality, and David and Goliath uses the avatar level when the enemy detaches. Damage accounting is deliberately a separate `World.damageDoneIncr` call at the recovered contact sites: nominal direct damage counts before protection, while beam, orbital and area damage do not. The source counter has no discovered UI/save consumer, so it stays session-local. Friendly/enemy accepted shot births are counted separately, and collected statistics count objects independently of their healing value.

`services/profile.saveCreatedTank` makes every valid creator save a fresh local ID, preserves previous saved designs, clears the old encoded provenance, and checks the three-retained-custom-design Tank Creator condition. Imported custom designs contribute; builtin duplicates do not. Local persistent medals remain an offline replacement for retired portal unlock calls. Browser services stay outside the simulation.


`tools/import-projectile-geometry.ts` recovers numerical sprite placements, shape/morph bounds, representative fill/line colors and line widths for34 projectile roots,53 sprites and79 leaves. It exports no vector paths or media. `assets/projectile-geometry.ts` composes those facts with retained poses, root rotation/scale, dynamic beam extents and turret facing. Script AABBs keep invisible helpers and declared morph start bounds, while visible procedural primitives exclude transparent helpers and honor animated morph ratios. Known empty frames stay empty; unknown future symbols retain a generic fallback.

`assets/mock-projectile.ts` builds cached procedural ellipse polygons, with paired Flak cells, clipped mask bounds and bubble details. Painting and point contact share the same transformed polygon silhouettes, so shot interception does not fall back to a universal radius2. Cached per-polygon rectangles reject distant contact queries cheaply. `render/mock-projectile-view.ts` paints the recovered palette and keeps strokes inside the declared extent. The procedural contours, representative gradient colors and rectangular mask constraints approximate the supplied artwork; they do not reproduce its paths, filters or antialiasing. `assets/mock-part.ts` supplies procedural leaf paint and frozen weapon posters, with a generic blue-body fallback for missing artwork. The native SWF path retains its vector/raster artwork and alpha-mask collision.

`tools/import-part-geometry.ts` recovers numeric idle layouts for the 73 non-body catalog parts. `assets/mock-part.ts` consumes their placement matrices, bounds, circles, alpha and uniform tint when painting procedural weapons/modules. Invisible muzzle helpers affect bounds alone. The imported facts stay separate from paint and simulation; class/creator code keeps the existing unpadded placement-radius convention. Body paint remains separate fidelity work.

`assets/part-snapshot.ts` constructs retained poster trees with independent recognized frame actions and repeatable private randomness. Class snapshots instead stop each body root at frame2. `AssetPack.rasterClip` composes those retained child poses; raw `rasterSymbol` access keeps its explicit authored-frame meaning. `assets/class-measurement.ts` measures only body artwork, using transformed leaf bounds and RGB-on-black capture with the original padding and inclusive class thresholds. `TankCreator` consumes this browser artwork service; simulation and serialized-design validation remain separate.

Shared `Dialog` focus setup/restoration runs in React's layout phase. --- title: TypeScript description: Next.js provides a TypeScript-first development experience for building your React application. --- {/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `Content` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */} Next.js comes with built-in TypeScript, automatically installing the necessary packages and configuring the proper settings when you create a new project with `create-next-app`. To add TypeScript to an existing project, rename a file to `.ts` / `.tsx`. Run `next dev` and `next build` to automatically install the necessary dependencies and add a `tsconfig.json` file with the recommended config options. > **Good to know**: If you already have a `jsconfig.json` file, copy the `paths` compiler option from the old `jsconfig.json` into the new `tsconfig.json` file, and delete the old `jsconfig.json` file. ## Using TypeScript 7 [TypeScript 7](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) does not currently provide the JavaScript compiler API. To use TypeScript 7 during `next build`, install it in your project: ```bash package="pnpm" pnpm add -D typescript@^7 ``` ```bash package="npm" npm install -D typescript@^7 ``` ```bash package="yarn" yarn add -D typescript@^7 ``` ```bash package="bun" bun add -D typescript@^7 ``` Next.js uses the project-local `tsc` CLI by default, so no additional configuration is required. To use the JavaScript compiler API instead, set [`experimental.useTypeScriptCli`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/useTypeScriptCli) to `false`. > **Good to know**: > > - CLI type checking prints the native `tsc` diagnostics. It does not apply Next.js-specific code frames or rewrite errors for routes, pages, layouts, or route handlers. > - The CLI checks the complete project selected by your `tsconfig` file. This includes test files and `.next/dev/types` when they are included by that configuration. [`next build --debug-build-paths`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-build-options) does not narrow the files that are type checked and produces a warning when used with this option. > - [`typescript.tsconfigPath`](#custom-tsconfig-path) continues to select the configuration passed to `tsc`. [`typescript.ignoreBuildErrors`](#disabling-typescript-errors-in-production) skips the type-checking step, including the CLI checker. > - `experimental.useTypeScriptCli` is experimental and its behavior may change. ## IDE Plugin Next.js includes a custom TypeScript plugin and type checker, which VSCode and other code editors can use for advanced type-checking and auto-completion. You can enable the plugin in VS Code by: 1. Opening the command palette (`Ctrl/⌘` + `Shift` + `P`) 2. Searching for "TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version" 3. Selecting "Use Workspace Version" Now, when editing files, the custom plugin will be enabled. By default, the project-local `tsc` CLI is used when running `next build`. Set [`experimental.useTypeScriptCli`](#using-typescript-7) to `false` to use the custom type checker instead. The TypeScript plugin can help with: - Warning if invalid values for [segment config options](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config) are passed. - Showing available options and in-context documentation. - Ensuring the `'use client'` directive is used correctly. - Ensuring client hooks (like `useState`) are only used in Client Components. > **🎥 Watch:** Learn about the built-in TypeScript plugin → [YouTube (3 minutes)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pqMqn9fKEf8) ## End-to-End Type Safety The Next.js App Router has **enhanced type safety**. This includes: 1. **No serialization of data between fetching function and page**: You can `fetch` directly in components, layouts, and pages on the server. This data _does not_ need to be serialized (converted to a string) to be passed to the client side for consumption in React. Instead, since `app` uses Server Components by default, we can use values like `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, and more without any extra steps. Previously, you needed to manually type the boundary between server and client with Next.js-specific types. 2. **Streamlined data flow between components**: With the removal of `_app` in favor of root layouts, it is now easier to visualize the data flow between components and pages. Previously, data flowing between individual `pages` and `_app` were difficult to type and could introduce confusing bugs. With [colocated data fetching](/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data) in the App Router, this is no longer an issue. [Data Fetching in Next.js](/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data) now provides as close to end-to-end type safety as possible without being prescriptive about your database or content provider selection. We're able to type the response data as you would expect with normal TypeScript. For example: ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher async function getData() { const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/...') // The return value is *not* serialized // You can return Date, Map, Set, etc. return res.json() } export default async function Page() { const name = await getData() return '...' } ``` For _complete_ end-to-end type safety, this also requires your database or content provider to support TypeScript. This could be through using an [ORM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object%E2%80%93relational_mapping) or type-safe query builder. ## Route-Aware Type Helpers Next.js generates global helpers for App Router route types. These are available without imports and are generated during `next dev`, `next build`, or via [`next typegen`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-typegen-options): - [`PageProps`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#page-props-helper) - [`LayoutProps`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#layout-props-helper) - [`RouteContext`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route#route-context-helper) ## `next-env.d.ts` Next.js generates a `next-env.d.ts` file in your project root. This file references Next.js type definitions, allowing TypeScript to recognize non-code imports (images, stylesheets, etc.) and Next.js-specific types. Running `next dev`, `next build`, or [`next typegen`](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-typegen-options) regenerates this file. > **Good to know**: > > - `next-env.d.ts` is managed by Next.js. Its contents are an implementation detail and may change over time. Add it to `.gitignore`. If your project already tracks the file, remove it from Git. Do not edit this file manually. > - The file must be in your `tsconfig.json` `include` array (`create-next-app` does this automatically). ## Examples ### Type Checking Next.js Configuration Files You can use TypeScript and import types in your Next.js configuration by using `next.config.ts`. ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { /* config options here */ } export default nextConfig ``` Module resolution in `next.config.ts` is currently limited to CommonJS. However, ECMAScript Modules (ESM) syntax is available when [using Node.js native TypeScript resolver](#using-nodejs-native-typescript-resolver-for-nextconfigts) for Node.js v22.10.0 and higher. When using the `next.config.js` file, you can add some type checking in your IDE using JSDoc as below: ```js filename="next.config.js" // @ts-check /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ const nextConfig = { /* config options here */ } module.exports = nextConfig ``` ### Using Node.js Native TypeScript Resolver for `next.config.ts` > **Note**: Available on Node.js v22.10.0+ and only when the feature is enabled. Next.js does not enable it. Next.js detects the [Node.js native TypeScript resolver](https://nodejs.org/api/typescript.html) via [`process.features.typescript`](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#processfeaturestypescript), added in **v22.10.0**. When present, `next.config.ts` can use native ESM, including top‑level `await` and dynamic `import()`. This mechanism inherits the capabilities and limitations of Node's resolver. In Node.js versions **v22.18.0+**, `process.features.typescript` is enabled by default. For versions between **v22.10.0** and **22.17.x**, opt in with `NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-transform-types`: ```bash filename="Terminal" NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-transform-types next ``` #### For CommonJS Projects (Default) Although `next.config.ts` supports native ESM syntax in CommonJS projects, Node.js will still assume `next.config.ts` is a CommonJS file by default, resulting in Node.js reparsing the file as ESM when module syntax is detected. Therefore, we recommend using the `next.config.mts` file for CommonJS projects to explicitly indicate it's an ESM module: ```ts filename="next.config.mts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' // Top-level await and dynamic import are supported const flags = await import('./flags.js').then((m) => m.default ?? m) const nextConfig: NextConfig = { /* config options here */ typedRoutes: Boolean(flags?.typedRoutes), } export default nextConfig ``` #### For ESM Projects When `"type"` is set to `"module"` in `package.json`, your project uses ESM. Learn more about this setting [in the Node.js docs](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#type). In this case, you can write `next.config.ts` directly with ESM syntax. > **Good to know**: When using `"type": "module"` in your `package.json`, all `.js` and `.ts` files in your project are treated as ESM modules by default. You may need to rename files with CommonJS syntax to `.cjs` or `.cts` extensions if needed. ### Statically Typed Links Next.js can statically type links to prevent typos and other errors when using `next/link`, improving type safety when navigating between pages. Works in both the Pages and App Router for the `href` prop in `next/link`. In the App Router, it also types `next/navigation` methods like `push`, `replace`, and `prefetch`. It does not type `next/router` methods in Pages Router. Literal `href` strings are validated, while non-literal `href`s may require a cast with `as Route`. To opt-into this feature, `typedRoutes` needs to be enabled and the project needs to be using TypeScript. ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { typedRoutes: true, } export default nextConfig ``` Next.js will generate a link definition in `.next/types` that contains information about all existing routes in your application, which TypeScript can then use to provide feedback in your editor about invalid links. > **Good to know**: If you set up your project without `create-next-app`, ensure the generated Next.js types are included by adding `.next/types/**/*.ts` to the `include` array in your `tsconfig.json`: {/* prettier-ignore-start */} ```json filename="tsconfig.json" highlight={4} { "include": [ "next-env.d.ts", ".next/types/**/*.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx" ], "exclude": ["node_modules"] } ``` {/* prettier-ignore-end */} Currently, support includes any string literal, including dynamic segments. For non-literal strings, you need to manually cast with `as Route`. The example below shows both `next/link` and `next/navigation` usage: ```tsx filename="app/example-client.tsx" 'use client' import type { Route } from 'next' import Link from 'next/link' import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation' export default function Example() { const router = useRouter() const slug = 'nextjs' return ( <> {/* Link: literal and dynamic */} {/* TypeScript error if href is not a valid route */} {/* Router: literal and dynamic strings are validated */} {/* For non-literal strings, cast to Route */} ) } ``` The same applies for redirecting routes defined by proxy: ```ts filename="proxy.ts" import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from 'next/server' export function proxy(request: NextRequest) { if (request.nextUrl.pathname === '/proxy-redirect') { return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/', request.url)) } return NextResponse.next() } ``` ```tsx filename="app/some/page.tsx" import type { Route } from 'next' import Link from 'next/link' export default function Page() { return Link Text } ``` To accept `href` in a custom component wrapping `next/link`, use a generic: ```tsx import type { Route } from 'next' import Link from 'next/link' function Card({ href }: { href: Route | URL }) { return (
My Card
) } ``` You can also type a simple data structure and iterate to render links: ```ts filename="components/nav-items.ts" import type { Route } from 'next' type NavItem = { href: T label: string } export const navItems: NavItem[] = [ { href: '/', label: 'Home' }, { href: '/about', label: 'About' }, { href: '/blog', label: 'Blog' }, ] ``` Then, map over the items to render `Link`s: ```tsx filename="components/nav.tsx" import Link from 'next/link' import { navItems } from './nav-items' export function Nav() { return (
{navItems.map((item) => ( {item.label} ))}
) } ``` > **How does it work?** > > When running, `next typegen`, `next dev` or `next build`, Next.js generates a hidden `.d.ts` file inside `.next` that contains information about all existing routes in your application (all valid routes as the `href` type of `Link`). This `.d.ts` file is included in `tsconfig.json` and the TypeScript compiler will check that `.d.ts` and provide feedback in your editor about invalid links. ### Type IntelliSense for Environment Variables During development, Next.js generates a `.d.ts` file in `.next/types` that contains information about the loaded environment variables for your editor's IntelliSense. If the same environment variable key is defined in multiple files, it is deduplicated according to the [Environment Variable Load Order](/docs/app/guides/environment-variables#environment-variable-load-order). To opt-into this feature, `experimental.typedEnv` needs to be enabled and the project needs to be using TypeScript. ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { experimental: { typedEnv: true, }, } export default nextConfig ``` > **Good to know**: Types are generated based on the environment variables loaded at development runtime, which excludes variables from `.env.production*` files by default. To include production-specific variables, run `next dev` with `NODE_ENV=production`. ### With Async Server Components To use an `async` Server Component with TypeScript, ensure you are using TypeScript `5.1.3` or higher and `@types/react` `18.2.8` or higher. If you are using an older version of TypeScript, you may see a `'Promise' is not a valid JSX element` type error. Updating to the latest version of TypeScript and `@types/react` should resolve this issue. ### Static Generation and Server-side Rendering For [`getStaticProps`](/docs/pages/api-reference/functions/get-static-props), [`getStaticPaths`](/docs/pages/api-reference/functions/get-static-paths), and [`getServerSideProps`](/docs/pages/api-reference/functions/get-server-side-props), you can use the `GetStaticProps`, `GetStaticPaths`, and `GetServerSideProps` types respectively: ```tsx filename="pages/blog/[slug].tsx" import type { GetStaticProps, GetStaticPaths, GetServerSideProps } from 'next' export const getStaticProps = (async (context) => { // ... }) satisfies GetStaticProps export const getStaticPaths = (async () => { // ... }) satisfies GetStaticPaths export const getServerSideProps = (async (context) => { // ... }) satisfies GetServerSideProps ``` > **Good to know:** `satisfies` was added to TypeScript in [4.9](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-9.html). We recommend upgrading to the latest version of TypeScript. ### With API Routes The following is an example of how to use the built-in types for API routes: ```ts filename="pages/api/hello.ts" import type { NextApiRequest, NextApiResponse } from 'next' export default function handler(req: NextApiRequest, res: NextApiResponse) { res.status(200).json({ name: 'John Doe' }) } ``` You can also type the response data: ```ts filename="pages/api/hello.ts" import type { NextApiRequest, NextApiResponse } from 'next' type Data = { name: string } export default function handler( req: NextApiRequest, res: NextApiResponse ) { res.status(200).json({ name: 'John Doe' }) } ``` ### With custom `App` If you have a [custom `App`](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/custom-app), you can use the built-in type `AppProps` and change file name to `./pages/_app.tsx` like so: ```ts import type { AppProps } from 'next/app' export default function MyApp({ Component, pageProps }: AppProps) { return } ``` ### Incremental type checking Since `v10.2.1` Next.js supports [incremental type checking](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#incremental) when enabled in your `tsconfig.json`, this can help speed up type checking in larger applications. ### Custom `tsconfig` path In some cases, you might want to use a different TypeScript configuration for builds or tooling. To do that, set `typescript.tsconfigPath` in `next.config.ts` to point Next.js to another `tsconfig` file. ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { typescript: { tsconfigPath: 'tsconfig.build.json', }, } export default nextConfig ``` For example, switch to a different config for production builds: ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const isProd = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { typescript: { tsconfigPath: isProd ? 'tsconfig.build.json' : 'tsconfig.json', }, } export default nextConfig ```
Why you might use a separate `tsconfig` for builds You might need to relax checks in scenarios like monorepos, where the build also validates shared dependencies that don't match your project's standards, or when loosening checks in CI to continue delivering while migrating locally to stricter TypeScript settings (and still wanting your IDE to highlight misuse). For example, if your project uses `useUnknownInCatchVariables` but some monorepo dependencies still assume `any`: ```json filename="tsconfig.build.json" { "extends": "./tsconfig.json", "compilerOptions": { "useUnknownInCatchVariables": false } } ``` This keeps your editor strict via `tsconfig.json` while allowing the production build to use relaxed settings.
> **Good to know**: > > - IDEs typically read `tsconfig.json` for diagnostics and IntelliSense, so you can still see IDE warnings while production builds use the alternate config. Mirror critical options if you want parity in the editor. > - In development, only `tsconfig.json` is watched for changes. If you edit a different file name via `typescript.tsconfigPath`, restart the dev server to apply changes. > - The configured file is used in `next dev`, `next build`, and `next typegen`. ### Disabling TypeScript errors in production Next.js fails your **production build** (`next build`) when TypeScript errors are present in your project. If you'd like Next.js to dangerously produce production code even when your application has errors, you can disable the built-in type checking step. If disabled, be sure you are running type checks as part of your build or deploy process, otherwise this can be very dangerous. Open `next.config.ts` and enable the `ignoreBuildErrors` option in the [`typescript`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/typescript) config: ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next' const nextConfig: NextConfig = { typescript: { // !! WARN !! // Dangerously allow production builds to successfully complete even if // your project has type errors. // !! WARN !! ignoreBuildErrors: true, }, } export default nextConfig ``` > **Good to know**: You can run `tsc --noEmit` to check for TypeScript errors yourself before building. This is useful for CI/CD pipelines where you'd like to check for TypeScript errors before deploying. ### Custom type declarations When you need to declare custom types, you might be tempted to modify `next-env.d.ts`. However, this file is automatically generated, so any changes you make will be overwritten. Instead, you should create a new file, let's call it `new-types.d.ts`, and reference it in your `tsconfig.json`: ```json filename="tsconfig.json" { "compilerOptions": { "skipLibCheck": true //...truncated... }, "include": [ "new-types.d.ts", "next-env.d.ts", ".next/types/**/*.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx" ], "exclude": ["node_modules"] } ``` ## Version Changes | Version | Changes | | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `v15.0.0` | [`next.config.ts`](#type-checking-nextjs-configuration-files) support added for TypeScript projects. | | `v13.2.0` | Statically typed links are available in beta. | | `v12.0.0` | [SWC](/docs/architecture/nextjs-compiler) is now used by default to compile TypeScript and TSX for faster builds. | | `v10.2.1` | [Incremental type checking](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#incremental) support added when enabled in your `tsconfig.json`. | # Architecture ## Engine choice [PixiJS](https://pixijs.com/8.x/guides/components/application) supplies the WebGL renderer and scene graph. The game does not need a rigid-body physics engine, a tile map, or an entity framework: the recovered simulation uses authored tank parts, point-against-art collision, independent velocity axes, and frame timers. Keeping those rules in plain TypeScript avoids coupling them to a framework's physics or variable-time integration. Next.js supplies the application shell, TypeScript build, and static delivery. Tailwind is installed through its PostCSS integration; stage-specific styling is kept in one stylesheet so original Flash coordinates can remain explicit. Pixi is imported on demand by rendered screens. No server-side game API or database is required. ## Ownership and flow 1. `AssetGate` accepts a local file or initializes procedural mock artwork. 2. `AssetPack` extracts images, sounds, vectors, font outlines, and sprite placements. Do not multiply recovered constants by wall-clock delta. - The stage is 550 × 450; rendering scales to fit without changing world dimensions. - Health and progression are the same resource. Kills alone do not grant XP. - The level life curve is `[50, 100, 170, 250, 400, 800, 2000]`. - Mounted primary cooldowns are independent; secondaries share their maximum mounted rate. - Field persistence owns living enemies and their exact runtime state. Inactive fields do not keep simulating. - Recovered catalog designs are immutable templates. Runtime health, timers, removed carrier parts, and hidden bubbles live on `Tank` instances. - Flash artwork is optional input. Mock mode must remain playable without a file. - Map connections are completed traversal history, independent of grid adjacency and field generation. Each unordered pair is stored once. Cleared fields remain valid destinations. - Camera zoom changes renderer scale and inverse pointer mapping together; simulation coordinates and the fixed HUD keep their original dimensions. ## Extending the game - Add a part definition in the catalog, an implementation in the relevant combat/AI system, and a recovered symbol or mock view.
